cards.headline: French authorities detained approximately 15,000 people during cost-of-living and high school protests

pages.text: French Justice Minister Gerald Darmanin told parliament that police arrested or detained about 15,000 people during recent protests involving high school students and demonstrations over the cost of living. The figure includes 7,184 people detained during protests regarding inflation and salaries since October 17, and approximately 8,000 people held during high school student protests over school conditions since September. Darmanin noted that protests on October 17, which involved serious riots in several cities, accounted for about two thirds of the arrests and detentions related to the cost-of-living demonstrations.

Regarding the 7,184 people detained during cost-of-living protests, Darmanin reported that 4,523 of those arrested were adults and 2,661 were minors, with five minors remaining in custody. Of these cases, 3,053 resulted in charges. Prison terms have been ordered in 666 cases, including 195 individuals sent straight to prison and others receiving suspended terms. In the separate high school student protests, Darmanin stated that only three people had been kept in detention, all of whom were adults accused of assaulting teachers or police.

cards.headline: UN human rights office warns of continued 'atrocious abuses' in Haiti

pages.text: The United Nations human rights office (OHCHR) has urged for greater civilian protection in Haiti as gangs continue to commit “atrocious abuses” amid intensified security operations. OHCHR spokesperson Marta Hurtado told journalists in Geneva that between January and 31 October, the office documented 4,595 people killed and 2,050 injured due to armed violence. This figure includes 1,167 killed and 459 injured between July and September. While Ms. Hurtado noted that some numbers “have gone down a little” compared to previous years, she stated that killings, rapes, and child recruitment by gangs remain “awfully high.”

Sexual violence remains a critical issue in Haiti. Between July and September, at least 340 women and girls were subjected to sexual violence, primarily gang rape. This brings the total number of documented cases from January to September to 1,497, with victims ranging in age from seven to 80. Referring to a report issued in February, Ms. Hurtado cited instances of mothers stating they preferred to give their daughters to gang members to ensure they were only raped rather than gang raped.

Violent armed groups maintain control over large areas of Haiti’s capital, Port-au-Prince, and other regions. Although the UN Security Council has authorized a Gang Suppression Force, the group has yet to be fully deployed. As security operations increase, gangs have adapted their tactics by carrying out retaliatory attacks on residents suspected of cooperating with security forces, conducting targeted kidnappings, increasing the forced recruitment of children and young people, and placing tighter restrictions on freedom of movement.

cards.headline: Iraqi Prime Minister to visit Lebanon to discuss diversifying oil export routes

pages.text: Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi is set to visit Beirut, Lebanon, to hold high-level meetings aimed at boosting economic cooperation and discussing the diversification of oil export routes. The visit follows disruptions to the Strait of Hormuz, a major energy waterway, caused by the US-Israel war on Iran that began in late February. Al-Zaidi is expected to meet with Lebanese President Joseph Aoun, Prime Minister Nawaf Salam, and Parliament Speaker Nabih Berri to discuss bilateral trade, customs exemption deals, and coordination on security and countering drug trafficking. A central part of the discussions is expected to involve a proposed project to link the Iraqi city of Kirkuk to Tripoli in northern Lebanon via a pipeline through Syria’s Mediterranean port of Baniyas. This project aims to potentially bypass the Strait of Hormuz, which carries approximately one-fifth of the world’s energy during peacetime but has faced severe disruption since the conflict began.

Iraq is seeking alternative routes for crude oil exports following the impact of the war in Iran on Gulf exports. According to Iraq’s Ministry of Oil, crude oil exports reached about 2.7 million barrels per day (bpd), an increase from some 200,000 bpd in May. Before the war, Iraq was exporting about 3.5 million bpd. The recent increase in export volume has been supported by the resumption of oil pumping through the Iraqi-Turkish pipeline at an initial capacity of 120,000 bpd. Walid Marrouch, a professor of economics at the Lebanese American University in Beirut, told Al Jazeera that Iraq is looking for alternative routes to diversify exports following the situation in Hormuz. While Iraq has previously looked to Syria for export alternatives, such efforts were difficult due to international sanctions under the leadership of Bashar al-Assad, who was toppled in late 2024.

cards.headline: Israeli military incursion into southwestern Syria causes shelling and residential damage

pages.text: Israeli troops conducted an incursion into southwestern Syria, involving shelling and gunfire that caused residential damage and forced families to flee, according to Syrian media reports. The operation, which reportedly began around midnight and lasted until approximately 2 a.m., targeted areas in the Daraa Governorate, including the villages of Maariya, Abidin, and Koya. While local news website Daraa24 reported no casualties, the incursion involved military vehicles, drones, and helicopters. Syrian officials have called for international action to stop these incursions, stating that military force cannot legitimize occupation. Since the fall of the Bashar al-Assad regime in December 2024, Israel has expanded its military presence in the buffer zone between Syria and the occupied Golan Heights and advanced into parts of southern Syria, despite the 1974 Disengagement of Forces Agreement.

In the village of Maariya, state-run TV news channel Al-Ekhbariya reported that a convoy of 23 Israeli military vehicles entered the area, where soldiers searched homes and fired into the air. In an area between Maariya and the village of Abidin, troops reportedly beat an elderly man and damaged his vehicle. The operation extended to the neighboring village of Koya, where Mayor Amjad Suleiman said Israeli troops advanced into farmland west of the village from the direction of Maariya before firing toward residences. Suleiman stated that Israeli forces opened indiscriminate and brutal fire on homes, causing one house to burn down completely. SANA news agency reported that an Israeli helicopter also fired heavy machine guns at a house in Koya, setting it on fire. Daraa24 reported that gunfire set a room in one house on fire and that Israeli forces fired five shells at the area around Koya. Al-Ekhbariya reported that Israeli troops stationed at the Al-Jazira barracks in western Daraa fired toward farmland between Koya and Maariya, where two artillery shells detonated, and that helicopters fired toward the plains surrounding Koya.

On November 17, 2026, Syria's Foreign Ministry condemned repeated raids in the Quneitra and Daraa Governorates and attacks on civilians, including women, children, and elderly people. The ministry accused Israeli forces of violating international law, disrupting livelihoods, and restricting access to land. The statement followed Israeli shelling of farmland near Koya and Abidin in western Daraa overnight. The ministry reaffirmed Damascus's sovereignty over the entire country and urged the international community to press Israel to halt the incursions, warning that continued attacks threaten regional stability and prospects for peace. These attacks followed an Israeli raid on Maariya on the evening of November 16, 2026, during which troops searched homes, beat a resident, and smashed his car, according to SANA.

cards.headline: Ukrainian drones and missiles strike Kerch Bridge linking Russia to occupied Crimea

pages.text: Ukrainian drones and missiles struck the Kerch Bridge, a vital link connecting the Russian mainland to the occupied Crimean Peninsula, according to Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy. Zelenskyy described the strike as an “unprecedented” operation that served as the seventh stage of a mission carried out over several weeks. The attack targeted the bridge over the Kerch Strait, a structure used to move military and civilian supplies from Russia to Crimea and to support troops on the front line. The bridge, completed in 2018, is considered a symbol of Russia's 2014 annexation of the peninsula. While the Ukrainian General Staff did not provide specific details on the extent of the damage, they stated that an arch and a span of the bridge's road section collapsed, severing the road link. The railway line remained standing, though it sustained damage to an arch. Russia's Investigative Committee, the nation's top criminal investigation agency, confirmed the bridge was attacked by drones and sustained damage but did not elaborate on the specifics.

The strike on the Kerch Bridge occurred amid an escalation in aerial attacks. While Ukraine targeted the bridge, Moscow's forces fired ballistic missiles and drones at Kyiv, hitting two of the Ukrainian capital's main bridges. Kyiv Mayor Vitaliy Klitschko reported damage to critical infrastructure systems and disruptions to heating and water supplies. At least two people were killed in the attacks on Kyiv. President Zelenskyy stated the bridge operation followed a weeks-long effort to gradually wear down Russian air defenses before the final bombardment. He identified the weaponry used in the culminating attacks as Ukrainian-made Neptune and Flamingo FP-5 cruise missiles, Palianytsia rocket drones, and Ruta cruise missiles from the Dutch manufacturer Destinus. Simultaneously, Russia reported that its forces downed a record number of Ukrainian drones for the second straight day.

cards.headline: Student List movement enters Serbia's parliament following election victory

pages.text: The Student List, a grassroots student-led movement, has entered Serbia's new parliament in Belgrade following an October 25 vote. Hundreds of supporters cheered the new lawmakers as they entered the National Assembly for the first time. The movement, which was backed by 2.3 million citizens, won the largest single share of the vote, removing President Aleksandar Vucic and his Serbian Progressive Party (SNS) from their previous position. The Student List holds a majority with 140 seats in the 250-member parliament, while the Serbian Progressive Party holds 104 seats.

The new parliamentary session is currently chaired by the oldest member of parliament until a new speaker is elected, with assistance from the four youngest MPs from the largest electoral lists. The formal agenda includes verifying parliamentary mandates based on a report by the Republic Electoral Commission (RIK), taking the solemn oath of office, electing the speaker and deputy speakers, appointing the secretary-general, and forming parliamentary committees and permanent delegations to international bodies. A new speaker could be announced later.

cards.headline: UK sanctions eight Israeli firms over West Bank settlement construction

pages.text: The United Kingdom has imposed sanctions on eight Israeli construction and property development firms involved in building settlements in the occupied West Bank. The British government stated the measures are intended to disrupt the financing and ability of these companies to support construction in the territory. This represents the first package of sanctions issued since the UK government announced a tougher approach toward Israeli actions in the West Bank. Settlement construction is considered illegal under international law, and such activity, along with settler attacks on Palestinians and their property, has risen sharply in recent years. The UK government's move aims to protect the prospect of a two-state solution, a political framework involving two independent states for Israelis and Palestinians. UK Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband has specifically criticized development plans in the E1 area east of Jerusalem, stating they would render a two-state solution unviable by cutting through the heart of Palestine. The E1 development plans, which have faced international condemnation, would effectively divide the West Bank in two and disconnect it from East Jerusalem.

The Palestinian foreign ministry welcomed the sanctions and urged other countries to follow the UK's lead. The announcement occurred two days before the deadline for bids for construction tenders in the E1 area. Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Saar criticized the sanctions on X, describing them as a “hostile act targeting private, law-abiding companies.” Saar stated that Israel will not change its policies or bow to external pressure and will respond with “countermeasures,” noting that decisions regarding these responses will be announced in due course. He added that Israel would consider new ways to strengthen Jewish communities in the West Bank and protect those involved in building and developing. Israel has previously condemned UK sanctions related to West Bank settlements, accusing the Labour government of “systematically acting against the State of Israel.”

cards.headline: Canada and China expand trade deal to provide roughly $400 million in tariff relief

pages.text: Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney and Chinese President Xi Jinping agreed to deepen economic and trade ties during a bilateral meeting in Shenzhen, China. The expanded deal provides tariff relief on Canadian exports worth roughly $400 million, including various pork and seafood products. In exchange for this relief, Canada agreed to ease some steel and aluminum tariffs. The announcement follows Carney's arrival at Shenzhen Bao'an International Airport on November 23, 2026, ahead of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit.

The expanded tariff removal includes several specific seafood categories: $87.5 million for certain frozen cold-water shrimp and prawns, including Pacific spot prawn; $61.4 million for certain molluscs, including geoduck; $39.4 million for sea cucumber; and $96 million for Greenland halibut. This follows a January agreement between Carney and Xi that saw China drop 25 per cent tariffs on lobster and crab. On Nov. 4, the federal government announced that China would extend the soon-to-expire tariff-free treatment for another two years. In 2024, approximately 16 per cent of Canada's fish and seafood exports went to China.

The trade measures also impact agricultural sectors. Canola meal and peas received the same January relief and extension as lobster and crab, which stopped 100 per cent tariffs on those products. Additionally, the deal opens market access for Canadian fava beans, chickpeas, and lentils to China. Bill Prybylski, the president of the Agricultural Producers Association of Saskatchewan, stated that the federal government's announcement is great news for canola producers.

cards.headline: Nvidia board refuses to reinstate Jensen Huang following resignation and scandal

pages.text: Nvidia's board of directors has stated it does not intend to reinstate ousted co-founder Jensen Huang as CEO, despite Huang expressing interest in returning to lead the company. During a call with financial analysts on November 17, 2026, Nvidia chair Harvey Jones said the board had “unanimously accepted” Huang's resignation and “does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO.” This decision follows Huang's resignation on November 12, 2026, after alleged extramarital affairs were revealed, including one involving a woman suspected of being a Chinese intelligence asset. Huang, 63, co-founded the company and led it for more than three decades, transforming it from a graphics card maker into a dominant supplier of chips used to train and operate advanced AI systems. In a post on X, Huang acknowledged making “serious mistakes in his personal life” and failing to meet expected standards, noting he had received calls from employees, investors, and partners asking him to return. While figures such as Elon Musk and US President Donald Trump called for his return as part of a “Bring Jensen Back” campaign, the company is moving forward under interim leadership.

Despite the leadership transition, Nvidia reported significant financial growth for the quarter ending October 25. The company's quarterly sales doubled from a year earlier to reach $115.8bn (£86.9bn), and profits also doubled from a year ago to hit $65bn. Data center revenue, a major component of the business, doubled to $107bn during the same period. Following these results, Nvidia shares rose by 4.8% in after-hours trading. Interim chief executive and CFO Colette Kress told investors that it is “business as usual” and stated, “We've got this.” Kress noted that the company's momentum is driven by the innovation of its people but did not address the specifics of Huang's resignation or the search for a permanent successor. Looking ahead, Nvidia stated it expects revenue to rise by another 13% in the next quarter. Daniela Hathorn, a senior analyst for trading platform Capital.com, noted that these results address concerns regarding cooling demand for AI infrastructure and suggest that Huang may not be irreplaceable as a leader.

cards.headline: Ecuadorian fishermen sue Trump administration over drone strike that sank vessel

pages.text: Sixteen fishermen from Ecuador filed a lawsuit in a Pennsylvania federal court on November 16, 2026, against the administration of U.S. President Donald Trump. The group alleges a drone strike sank their vessel, the La Negra Francisca Duarte II, on March 17 and caused injuries to the crew. The lawsuit seeks financial restitution for the fishermen and asks the court to order an end to the Trump administration’s campaign of strikes targeting boats in the Caribbean and eastern Pacific that the U.S. claims are involved in drug trafficking.

The crew of the La Negra Francisca Duarte II reported that the boat was attacked by drones launched from a U.S.-operated vessel. According to lawyer Dan Kovalik, the attack left at least two crewmembers with severe burns and caused trauma to all members. The complaint also alleges the crew faced arbitrary arrest, torture, and forced transfer to El Salvador by U.S. military personnel. Captain Hernan Flores told Reuters that the boat was the crew's only livelihood and that they received no help from anyone in Ecuador.

The U.S. government has not claimed responsibility for the strike on the La Negra Francisca Duarte II or two other Ecuadorian vessels that were reportedly attacked and sunk in recent months. While the Trump administration has denied involvement in this specific attack, it defends its broader bombing campaign against alleged drug-running vessels in the eastern Pacific and the Caribbean, stating the mission aims to halt narcotics flow into the United States. A report from the Washington Post in August suggested the vessels may have been targeted by the CIA as part of a secret overseas mission, though other reports suggest the attacks could have been conducted by a regional ally or a U.S. government contractor.

cards.headline: IRGC Quds Force commander arrives in Iraq to mediate tensions over suspected oil smuggling

pages.text: Esmail Qaani, the head of Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) Quds Force, has arrived in Iraq to seek a solution to rising tensions near Jurf al-Nasr, an Iraqi town located near Baghdad. An Iraqi official told Al Jazeera that Qaani met with Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi and held meetings with forces within the Coordination Framework—an umbrella group for Shia Iraqi parties in the Iraqi parliament—to reach an agreement regarding an investigation into suspected oil smuggling. The tensions center on Jurf al-Nasr, which is a stronghold of the pro-Iranian armed group Kataib Hezbollah. A leaked intelligence report indicated that two strategic oil pipelines running through the town had effectively been tapped into. While the Iraqi government has framed its recent anti-corruption crackdown in the area as an initiative to protect public funds from a smuggling network, some analysts believe the move is a strategy to sever the financial resources of pro-Iranian armed groups that have not integrated into the state apparatus. The town allegedly harbors illicit oil refineries.

On November 16, 2026, Prime Minister al-Zaidi instructed military and security commanders to deploy additional forces around Jurf al-Nasr and to prepare for government troops to enter the area. Security agencies have also been told to prevent tankers carrying oil or petroleum products from leaving the town. This order could potentially lead to a direct confrontation between Iraqi government troops and Kataib Hezbollah. An Iraqi official previously told Al Jazeera that Kataib Hezbollah has until to leave Jurf al-Nasr. According to Al Jazeera’s correspondent in Iraq, at least three leaders of the Coordination Framework have expressed rejection of any armed clash or the entry of federal forces before a political understanding is reached with Kataib Hezbollah. An Iraqi official told Al Jazeera that the judicial committee has not yet reached an agreement with the factions to enter the area.

cards.headline: United States loses measles elimination status amid worst outbreak since 1991

pages.text: The United States has lost its measles elimination status, an official recognition that the infectious disease is now endemic in the country after being eliminated for 26 years. The Pan American Health Organization (PAHO), a regional branch of the World Health Organization, announced the decision, which indicates the virus is continually spreading within the nation. Dr. Jarbas Barbosa da Silva Jr, the director of PAHO, made the final decision and stated that losing the status means the virus has circulated for a prolonged period, putting communities at risk of preventable illness, hospitalization, and death. The United States is among Bolivia and Mexico, which have also lost their measles elimination status as endemic transmission is re-established in those countries. PAHO considers transmission endemic when the same measles virus genotype and lineage circulate uninterrupted for 12 months or more in a country.

The loss of status follows the worst measles outbreak in the United States since 1991. As of November 12, the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention had confirmed 5,412 measles cases and 6 deaths. Other reports indicate that U.S. states have reported a total of 10 deaths from the virus, while some sources state that approximately 7,700 people have been infected and 13 have died since 2025. Pennsylvania has been reported as the worst-hit state, with more than 1,500 cases and seven measles-related deaths. Measles is one of the most contagious viruses known to medicine and requires 95% of a community to be vaccinated to prevent outbreaks.

Health authorities and medical groups have linked the resurgence to gaps in vaccination coverage. The American Medical Association, the nation's largest doctors group, described the loss of elimination status as a “deeply troubling and entirely preventable setback.” While the measles vaccine is safe and highly effective, pockets of low vaccination have grown in the U.S. following pandemic-era disruptions and widespread misinformation. Dr. Barbosa da Silva noted that measles is resurging globally due to persistent gaps in vaccination, a trend affecting the Americas. He characterized the declaration as largely symbolic with few practical implications, but called it a “serious warning” that can be reversed through sustained commitment to vaccination and surveillance.

cards.headline: Mozambique opposition leader Venâncio Mondlane faces terrorism charges in court

pages.text: Venâncio Mondlane, leader of the Anamola party in Mozambique, has appeared in court to face terrorism charges. The proceedings reopen tensions surrounding the country's disputed 2024 elections and have raised concerns regarding Mozambique's political stability. Mondlane finished second to President Daniel Chapo in an election that international observers said was marred by irregularities. Following that election, Mondlane mobilized thousands of supporters for months of protests. According to civil society groups, a violent security crackdown on those protests left at least 400 people dead.

Mondlane has rejected the charges and is questioning the legality of the case. He accused the Attorney General's Office of withholding the accusation for 130 days and argued that the documents presented contain serious procedural irregularities. pages.text: Iraq and Turkey resumed oil flows through a long-shuttered pipeline on November 17, 2026. cards.headline: Students' List candidates take seats in inaugural Serbian parliamentary session

pages.text: Candidates from the student-led Students' List have taken their oaths during the inaugural session of the Serbian parliament in Belgrade. This move serves as the first step for the youth-backed party toward forming a new government following the end of Aleksandar Vucic's 14-year rule. The Students' List holds 140 seats in the 250-member parliament, making them the new majority. The right-wing Serbian Progressive Party (SNS) holds 103 seats, while the remaining seats belong to ethnic minority parties. Once the parliament is formed, the Students' List has 90 days to name a prime minister, present a programme, and form a government.

Hundreds of people gathered outside the parliament building in Belgrade to support the new lawmakers, many of whom are teachers, professors, and other professionals with little or no political experience. In contrast, SNS candidates faced negative reactions from the crowd; one woman poured yogurt over an SNS member's head as the individual climbed the steps to the parliament entrance. cards.headline: Rights groups raise alarm as executions in Saudi Arabia reach at least 211 in 2026

pages.text: Human rights organizations are raising alarms over an intensifying crackdown on critics and a rising number of executions in Saudi Arabia. This follows the execution of two men in Saudi Arabia's Eastern Province on November 14, 2026: Jawad Abdullah Qureiris and Fadel Hassan al-Safwani. Saudi authorities stated both men were convicted of terrorist offenses. Fadel Hassan al-Safwani was a prominent organizer of peaceful protests in 2011 that called for civil rights and the release of detainees. Jawad Abdullah Qureiris participated in one of those protests in the city of Qatif while he was a minor. In November 2024, the UN Working Group on Arbitrary Detention called for Qureiris' release after finding his detention was arbitrary. Qureiris was the fourth of five men to be executed following an opinion that also covered four others.

cards.headline: Yemeni parliament unanimously approves law designating Houthis as terrorist organisation

pages.text: Yemen’s parliament has unanimously approved a 55-article law designating the Houthis—also known as Ansar Allah—as a “terrorist organisation” and a “rebellious faction.” The law, which criminalises the group’s activities and financing, was approved via videolink over two sessions on November 16, 2026. The legislation has been formally submitted to Rashad al-Alimi, head of the Yemeni Presidential Leadership Council, to be signed into law. This follows the Yemeni cabinet's approval of the draft law on October 11. The measure targets the group's political, military, and civilian formations as fighting intensifies between the group and forces loyal to the internationally recognised government. The law toughens penalties for several offences, including attacking international shipping, laying landmines, attacking civilians, besieging cities, and seizing state authority; certain offences under the law would carry the death penalty.

The parliamentary vote comes seven years after the measure was first proposed. The bill was originally tabled during a session in the city of Seiyun in April 2019, but parliament said it had deferred the bill at that time to give peace efforts a chance. Parliament noted that the Iranian-backed Houthis had attacked government-held areas of Yemen and Saudi Arabia, and accused the group of brushing aside “all options for peace.” While the parliament has now passed the law, the country’s National Defence Council had previously designated the Houthis a “terrorist” organisation by executive decision in October 2022. The United States and Saudi Arabia also list or treat the group as a “terrorist” organisation.

cards.headline: Ebola outbreak in DR Congo remains out of control six months after declaration

pages.text: An Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) continues to spread and kill at a record pace six months after it was declared on May 15. The outbreak, caused by the rare Bundibugyo strain of the virus, has infected more than 11,000 people and resulted in over 5,500 deaths, according to government data. This is the deadliest of the country's 17 recorded outbreaks and is on track to surpass the death toll of the West African outbreak that killed 11,000 people between 2014 and 2016. Official data indicates that infections and deaths are rising at double the rate seen during the first six months of the 2014-2016 West African outbreak, which saw more than 28,600 infections and over 11,000 deaths according to the World Health Organisation (WHO). By the time the outbreak was announced in mid-May, 43 deaths had already been recorded, suggesting the virus had circulated undetected for an extended period. The disease has since spread to eight of the country's 26 provinces, moving at a pace aid groups have likened to wildfire.

Containment efforts are faltering due to resource shortages, insecurity, and poor coordination. The Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention reports that 80% of new cases are being detected outside health surveillance, meaning most infections have not been tracked by authorities. Community transmission remains high, with one-third of deaths occurring at home or in the community where burials and other procedures are often conducted without specialist supervision, increasing transmission risks. In Ituri province, the original epicentre, the medical charity Médecins Sans Frontières stated that vital resources and supplies are not reaching hotspots outside that area. Additionally, health workers, vehicles, and surveillance teams have come under attack in communities that distrust outsiders. WHO Director General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus identified insecurity as one of the greatest obstacles to the response, noting that delays are slowing efforts.

The response is further hampered by labor disputes and funding issues. Health workers have repeatedly gone on strike over conditions and unpaid salaries, with some officials stating that some workers have not been paid since August. These strikes have sometimes left patients with confirmed infections without treatment. While approximately $2.9 billion has been pledged for the response, Africa's top public health agency reports that less than half of that has been disbursed. cards.headline: Canada and China agree to further tariff cuts on seafood, pork, and steel

pages.text: Canada and China have announced new tariff cuts for various products, including seafood and steel, following a meeting between Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney and Chinese President Xi Jinping at an Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in Shenzhen. The agreement builds on a January deal intended to reduce mutual trade barriers and repair diplomatic relations. This move is part of Prime Minister Carney's efforts to reduce Canada's economic dependence on the United States amid tariffs imposed by the U.S. administration.

Under the new measures, China will provide tariff relief for approximately CAN$400 million in Canadian exports. This includes CAN$116 million in exports of frozen pork cuts and CAN$285 million in fish and seafood. In exchange, Canada has agreed to extend existing remission measures for certain Chinese steel and aluminium products—which were set to expire at the end of 2026—by two years. Canada will also add remissions to another 32 steel and aluminium items for which the country lacks sufficient supply. To date, Canada has restored market access for more than 90 percent of trade previously subject to tariffs, representing nearly CAN$7.5 billion ($5.2 billion) in Canadian exports, according to a statement from Carney’s office.

The expansion of trade follows a period of strained relations that began in 2018 after Canada arrested the daughter of Huawei’s founder on a U.S. warrant, leading to the retaliatory detention of two Canadians by China on espionage charges. President Xi Jinping described the current state of ties as a “turnaround,” stating that improving relations serves the interests of both countries and supports global stability. Prime Minister Carney stated that Canada is “well ahead of our schedule” to increase exports to China by 50 percent by the end of this decade. Under the January agreement, Canada also lowered its 100 percent tariff on Chinese electric vehicles to 6.1 percent, with an initial cap of 49,000 vehicles per year that is set to rise to 70,000 over five years.

cards.headline: UK foreign secretary announces first sanctions against Israeli firms in West Bank settlements

pages.text: UK Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband has announced the first set of sanctions against Israeli companies planning to build illegal settlements in the West Bank. The measures target eight identified construction, property development, and architectural businesses that have helped to plan, build, supply, or market housing and public infrastructure in Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank. The move is designed to stop the flow of finance to these firms and hinder the building of more settlements, which Miliband pledged to prevent to protect the chances of a two-state solution. Miliband also announced sanctions on a right-wing activist Israeli group involved in attempting to block aid into Gaza as recently as the announcement. The Foreign Office stated that the current Israeli government has “not only refused to clamp down on illegal settlement, but has facilitated and encouraged them,” noting that more settlements have been approved under the current government in four years than in the previous 20 years.

The sanctions were announced just before the Israeli government was due to allocate tenders for the large E1 West Bank settlement. While implementing these measures, Miliband expressed a desire to work with a new Israeli government in a more cooperative way. Gadi Eisenkot, Israel’s possible new prime minister, has stated that if appointed, he will take a tougher approach to settler violence than Benjamin Netanyahu. The Foreign Office distinguished activity in settlements from trade with “green line Israel,” stating it welcomes and encourages trade with the latter. These new sanctions follow an announcement on 8 September by Miliband regarding an expansion of the Global Human Rights sanctions regime and a set of measures, yet to be implemented, designed to ban the trade in goods from illegal settlements. cards.headline: Trump to raise Ukraine war in trilateral talks with Xi and Putin at APEC summit

pages.text: President Donald Trump intends to raise the war in Ukraine during an unprecedented trilateral meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in Shenzhen, China. While Trump has stated his intention to discuss Ukraine, administration officials have said the war will not be part of the discussions. The summit is also expected to focus on nuclear arms control and the war in Iran. This meeting between the leaders of the world's three largest nuclear powers marks a departure from Trump's first administration, which identified China and Russia as principal geopolitical competitors. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has expressed concern that major powers may discuss global spheres of influence without Ukraine present at the table.

The gathering in Shenzhen may signal a shift in how the United States approaches major global powers. Jonathan Czin, a former CIA China expert now at the Brookings Institution, noted that the subtext of the meeting may be more significant than its substance, suggesting US allies in Asia and Europe could view the administration as more focused on accommodating China and Russia than countering their influence. Czin described the meeting as a potential ``political coup'' for Putin, who would gain the opportunity to share the international stage with Trump and Xi despite Russia's isolation from much of the West. Separately, Trump is scheduled to hold talks with Xi Jinping during the November 18-19 gathering.

Regarding US-China relations, experts suggest the leaders may focus on stabilizing a fragile trade relationship rather than achieving major breakthroughs. Jia Hui Tee, a senior trade policy analyst at the Hinrich Foundation, noted that the leaders could potentially make progress on reciprocal tariff cuts covering goods worth $30 billion on each side, though a timeline has not been set. Washington is seeking for Beijing to accelerate purchases of US agricultural products and increase exports of rare earths and other critical minerals. However, Tee noted that China would likely be cautious with commitments, especially as Trump faces domestic pressure following Republican losses in the midterm elections. Zhang Lun, a professor at CY Cergy Paris University, added that strained ties with allies and the war in Iran have reduced America's leverage and influence.

cards.headline: Migrant arrivals to Spain's Canary Islands spike ahead of general election

pages.text: More than 11,000 migrants reached Spain’s Canary Islands during the first half of November, according to Spanish government figures. This increase follows a period earlier in the year when fewer migrants arrived at the archipelago, which serves as a major entry point for people attempting the Atlantic Ocean crossing from West and North Africa in makeshift boats. On November 15, 2026, Spain’s maritime rescue service assisted 1,324 people aboard 14 boats, most of whom arrived on the island of El Hierro. This arrival figure was close to the daily record for the Atlantic migration route set in November 2020. The surge in arrivals has placed pressure on reception and emergency services on smaller islands like El Hierro, which has a population of approximately 12,000 people.

The spike in arrivals coincides with Spain’s general election campaign ahead of the November 29 election. Santiago Abascal, leader of the far-right, anti-immigrant Vox party, called the arrivals “an invasion” during a campaign event on the night of November 16, 2026. Speaking to supporters on the island of Tenerife, Abascal stated, “Whoever enters Spain illegally will leave Spain and will never be made legal.” He also accused some of disguising themselves as defenders of the Canary Islands to spread problems throughout Spain. The ruling Socialist Party, led by Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez, has faced criticism from conservative politicians regarding immigration policies, including a push to legalize more than 1 million undocumented immigrants already in the country. Several opinion polls show the Socialist Party trailing the combined support of the conservative Popular Party and Vox.

The Canary Islands are a primary destination for migrants fleeing poverty and conflict in West and North Africa. José Antonio Rodríguez, a spokesperson for the regional Red Cross immediate response team, said most of those arriving are from Senegal, Mali, Gambia, and Guinea. This recent surge follows a significant migration event in July, when tens of thousands of people crossed from Morocco into the Spanish North African territory of Ceuta in just two days. That event resulted in more than 140 deaths. Between January and the end of October, more than 13,000 people reached the Canary Islands by sea, according to Spain’s Interior Ministry.

cards.headline: EU foreign ministers agree to revive cooperation deal with Syria

pages.text: European Union foreign ministers have agreed to revive a nearly 20-year-old cooperation deal with Syria to strengthen ties with the country following the collapse of the Bashar al-Assad government in December 2024. The decision, announced by EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas on November 16, 2026, aims to establish a framework for trade, political dialogue, and closer cooperation between Brussels and Damascus as soon as possible. Kallas stated that the bloc needs to engage with Syria to prevent a vacuum that could be filled by other players. Diplomats will now work through the technical and legal details to finalize the agreement and launch talks for an updated version of the deal.

The original EU-Syria association agreement was established in 2008 during the presidency of Bashar al-Assad, but it was never fully signed by either party due to concerns regarding the Assad government's human rights record. To secure an updated deal, Kallas said the EU would set new conditions, including clear conditionality regarding human rights and the nonrecognition of occupied Ukrainian and Georgian territories that were recognized under the Assad regime. A discussion paper prepared by the bloc's diplomatic service ahead of the meeting in Brussels described the move as one of the EU's most ambitious efforts to normalize ties with Syria less than two years after the fall of the previous government.

cards.headline: Guinean crackdown on illegal gold mining triggers mass displacement and regional tension

pages.text: A sudden ban on illegal artisanal mining in Guinea has caused a wave of displacement across West Africa and sparked a diplomatic dispute with neighboring Sahel states. Guinean authorities enforced the ban to curb deforestation and river pollution caused by large-scale illegal mining, particularly in the Siguiri area of the northeast. The crackdown has forced tens of thousands of people to flee, with Mali reporting that up to 160,000 miners have entered the Malian portion of the border town Kourémalé and traveled as far as the capital, Bamako. In the border town of Kourémalé, which is split between Guinea and Mali, thousands of families have been traveling across the frontier following the enforcement of the ban. At least six women have given birth in Mali since the displacement began in Guinea.

The enforcement of the mining ban has resulted in significant arrests and legal consequences. Security agents raided mining hotspots, confiscating equipment and arresting 1,263 people. In Conakry, the Court for the Repression of Economic and Financial Offenses issued several sentences: 22 former local officials from the Siguiri region were sentenced to two years in prison and fined 10 million Guinean francs each for complicity in environmental degradation, destruction, and water pollution. Additionally, 20 miners were sentenced to three years in prison for illegal mining and environmental offenses; several of these individuals are foreign nationals who were also banned from Guinean territory for 10 years. Other reports indicate a Conakry court jailed 202 people accused of illegal gold mining in the Siguiri region.

Violence and diplomatic friction have accompanied the crackdown. On 11 November, deadly clashes occurred in the Balato community in Siguiri between security agents and miners who had erected barricades. The violence left at least 10 people killed and 13 others wounded, and three military vehicles were set alight. The situation has created regional tension; in a statement released on 12 November following a meeting in Ouagadougou, the Alliance of Sahel States recognized the authority of countries to enforce their laws but expressed concern regarding the decree and the subsequent expulsions.

cards.headline: United States and Iran locked in stalemate after nearly nine months of war

pages.text: The United States and Iran are engaged in a stalemate nearly nine months into a war, with both nations acting as if they have time on their side. This calculation has created a situation that former US Middle East negotiators, European officials, and Gulf sources say is almost impossible for either side to break, and they warn that fighting could resume before a diplomatic exit is reached. US President Donald Trump has opted to squeeze Iran through economic pressure rather than resuming heavy military strikes or making concessions. Trump is relying on a naval blockade and economic pain to force Tehran to agree to concessions regarding its nuclear programme, having held off on renewed bombing due to concerns that it would not change the outcome and could trigger Iranian reprisals against energy infrastructure in the Gulf.

Iranian leaders have responded by raising the cost of a peace deal for the United States, demanding that Washington make the first move toward a resolution. Tehran says it is open to diplomacy and has been meeting with Omani and Qatari mediators, but the government accuses Washington of pursuing coercion and maintains it will not yield to US pressure. Dennis Ross, a former US Middle East negotiator, described a dual reality where neither side has good options, noting that each side is defining the requirements to end the war in ways that are contradictory to the other. A senior European official stated that Washington's demands are too costly for Iran to accept, while Tehran's demands are too politically costly for Washington. A second senior European official, briefed by a national intelligence agency, said the US military campaign had achieved the opposite of what was intended.

cards.headline: Iraq approves rehabilitation of oil pipeline to Türkiye as flows resume after 12 years

pages.text: Iraq’s Cabinet has approved a recommendation to rehabilitate the Iraq–Türkiye oil pipeline, following the resumption of crude oil flows through the route for the first time in 12 years. The decision was made during a Cabinet meeting chaired by Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi in the southern province of Najaf, according to a statement from his media office carried by the official Iraqi News Agency. The Cabinet approved the recommendation from the Ministerial Council for the Economy regarding the pipeline's rehabilitation, though the statement did not detail the specific provisions or the scope of work involved. The pipeline connects Iraq's northern oil-producing region to Türkiye’s Mediterranean port of Ceyhan and had been out of service since 2014 following repeated attacks by the terrorist group ISIS (Daesh).

The Iraqi Oil Ministry announced that pumping for export resumed through the original pipeline after the completion of technical and operational tests. Oil Minister Basim Mohammed Khudair stated that flows began at 120,000 barrels per day (bpd) and are expected to gradually rise to 500,000 bpd, though he provided no timeline for reaching that level. The Ministerial Council for the Economy reviewed the ministry’s crude export plan, which includes the resumption of Kirkuk exports through the pipeline to Ceyhan, and instructed the ministry to intensify export efforts. The Kirkuk pipeline has a capacity of more than 1.5 million bpd.

The reopening of this route provides Baghdad with an additional export outlet, which helps reduce the country's dependence on shipping oil through the Strait of Hormuz. Iraq is one of the nations most affected by competing blockades in the Strait of Hormuz, a waterway through which nearly all of Iraq’s oil exports exited prior to the US-Israeli war on Iran. In August, Iraq and Türkiye signed a one-year agreement to maintain oil flows through the Kirkuk-Ceyhan pipeline, providing for a transportation capacity of up to 750,000 bpd as the two countries pursue a broader long-term arrangement.

cards.headline: First unit of Rooppur Nuclear Power Plant begins trial electricity supply to Bangladesh national grid

pages.text: The first unit of the Rooppur Nuclear Power Plant began feeding electricity into the national grid of Bangladesh on a trial basis on November 17, 2026. The first grid synchronisation occurred at 3:16 p.m., marking a milestone for the Tk 1.39 lakh crore ($11.2 billion) project in Pabna. The facility, located on the banks of the Padma River approximately 160 km from Dhaka, was developed by the Russian state nuclear corporation Rosatom, which began construction of the two reactors in 2017. The 2.4-gigawatt plant is projected to supply around 11 percent of the country's electricity needs, which officials say will help reduce reliance on imported fossil fuels and ease pressure on foreign currency reserves. Bangladesh currently receives about half of its electricity from gas and has experienced chronic shortages, including during the fuel crisis sparked by the war in the Middle East.

During the initial trial phase, the unit supplied up to 350 megawatts (MW) of electricity before the science and technology ministry reduced the output to 300 MW to maintain grid stability. Project Director Md Kabir Hossain stated the initial grid connection would last approximately eight to 10 hours, after which the unit would be disconnected for further tests. Following a break of about 28 hours, the unit would be reconnected to initially supply electricity for four to six hours. These tests are designed to assess the performance of the turbine, generator, control systems, and the equipment connecting the plant to the national grid. While electricity generated during this testing period can be used by consumers, an uninterrupted supply cannot yet be guaranteed. The development does not mean the plant has entered commercial operation; Unit 1 must undergo several rounds of technical tests and regulatory checks before it can supply electricity commercially at full capacity.

Science and Technology Minister Fakir Mahbub Anam described the connection as a “historic achievement.” Project Director Md Kabir Hossain noted that the tests will determine how the grid handles the power and assess the impact on the turbine. He stated that based on current parameters, turbine vibration and grid frequency are normal, but the actual situation will become clear once the two are connected. The first 1.2-GW reactor is scheduled to become fully operational in 2027, with the second reactor to follow in 2028. While an exact date for regular transmission has not been determined due to technical issues, Hossain stated it will take place “very soon” according to preparations.

cards.headline: Community guardians in Zimbabwe reduce lion-human conflict

pages.text: The nonprofit Wildlife Conservation Action (WCA) has implemented a “community guardian” model to reduce human-wildlife conflict between African lions and local communities in Zimbabwe. Known as “Batabilili,” these trained guardians work to mitigate conflict by monitoring lion movement, conducting community meetings, and helping farmers secure livestock in above-ground kraals, which are enclosures used to protect animals. Moreangels Mbizah, a conservation biologist and founder of WCA, stated that the organization aims to provide emotional and psychological support to community members experiencing losses, addressing a perceived lack of support from wildlife authorities toward people living alongside wildlife.

The Batabilili model has resulted in significant reductions in conflict incidents. In two wards of the Nyaminyami rural district, where WCA began working six years ago, the organization has recorded a 98% reduction in conflict incidents. Additionally, conflict has decreased by 53% across the districts of Mbire and Binga. Mbizah noted that because the guardians are members of the communities—described as the children, brothers, and sisters of the residents—they are trusted to address concerns directly, which has helped reduce retaliatory killings of lions that prey on livestock.

cards.headline: Florida fungus found to contain both psychedelic compounds and deadly toxins

pages.text: The fungus *Galerina indica*, dubbed the “dark magic mushroom,” is the first species known to contain both mind-altering psychedelic chemicals and deadly toxins. Found in the wetlands of central Florida, the small brown mushroom produces the psychedelic compounds psilocybin and psilocin, alongside deadly amatoxins. While some mushrooms are known to contain either psychedelics or amatoxins, this discovery represents a rare convergence of both chemical properties in a single species. Findings regarding the fungus were published in the journal *Current Biology* on November 11.

Fungal biologist Andrew Kunik, a study co-author from the University of Florida, identified the species on a moss-covered palm trunk while studying fungi in central Florida in 2025. Kunik noted that the specimen turned blue when handled, which can be a sign of psilocybin production. To investigate, Kunik and colleagues performed chemical analyses on *G. indica* and specimens of two unnamed *Galerina* species collected in the southeastern United States between January 2024 and September 2025. The analysis confirmed that *G. indica* contained psilocybin, psilocin, and two amatoxins, including one toxin that had never been documented in mushrooms before.

cards.headline: European Court of Human Rights rules Turkey must release jailed lawmaker Can Atalay

cards.headline: Rare microbes in the Gulf of Mexico surge in population following oil spills

pages.text: Florida International University (FIU) biologist Shen Jean Lim discovered that microbes capable of consuming oil were virtually undetectable in the Gulf of Mexico one year before the Deepwater Horizon spill. Testing seawater samples collected by a NOAA crew in 2009, Lim found that the abundances of these microbes were much lower than her research team had predicted. While these microbes became incredibly abundant in the near immediate aftermath of the 2010 spill to break down the oil, they were not present in high numbers in the pre-spill environment. These findings, published in Applied and Environmental Microbiology, suggest these microbes exist in a hidden reservoir of rare organisms that surge in population only when a sudden flood of oil provides a food source.

Lim used the 2009 samples to create what she describes as the most detailed picture of the deep Gulf's microbial community prior to the largest marine oil spill in U.S. history. Previously, researchers only possessed data from during and after the spill, leaving the baseline state of the ecosystem unknown. Lim and her colleagues suggest that because these microbes act as first responders that increase in abundance the moment an ecosystem is disrupted, they could serve as early-warning sentinels for ocean health.

cards.headline: Garment workers in Bangladesh to receive revised pay in January

pages.text: Garment workers in Bangladesh will receive revised pay in January as their December wage once a new minimum wage structure is announced, according to Minimum Wage Board Chairman Syed Azad Subhani. Subhani made these remarks during an emergency press briefing at the Minimum Wage Board conference room in Dhaka, UNB reports. The government formed the Minimum Wage Board on November 1 to refix wages for garment workers following labour unrest. The board held its first meeting on November 4, where it agreed to implement a new wage structure.

During the board's second meeting on November 9, representatives for workers submitted a proposal demanding a minimum monthly wage of Tk 32,000 for RMG (ready-made garment) workers. Factory owners did not submit a proposal during that meeting; while owners requested seven working days to do so, the board provided a four-day deadline. The board's postponed third meeting has been rescheduled for November 23, at which time factory owners are set to present their proposed minimum wage, according to a board notification.
Addressing the delay of the third meeting, Chairman Subhani clarified that the meeting was postponed solely due to an issue concerning a permanent member, dismissing any other reasons for the delay.

cards.headline: Clean energy transition concessions cover an estimated 328 million hectares globally

pages.text: Commercial concessions for clean energy and critical transition minerals now span an estimated 328 million hectares (about 810.5 million acres) globally, an area equivalent to the size of India, according to a November report by the International Land Coalition (ILC) and the land monitoring initiative Land Matrix. The report indicates that the global push to transition away from fossil fuels is driving a surge in mineral extraction and renewable energy infrastructure that is reorganizing land use, resource flows, and geopolitical power relations. Approximately 80% of the total mapped area consists of projects in early exploration and planning phases, while roughly 20% of mapped projects are currently operational. Jérémy Bourgoin, a report co-author and leader of the ILC Knowledge & Research team, told Mongabay that the true scale of the energy transition's physical land footprint was previously unknown despite calls to fast-track the process.

The report breaks down the land use into two primary categories: mining concessions for critical minerals—such as copper, lithium, nickel, and cobalt—cover 239 million hectares (591 million acres), while large-scale solar, wind, hydro, and geothermal facilities account for 159 million hectares (393 million acres). Building low-carbon technologies requires more land and raw materials than traditional fossil fuel systems. For example, an electric vehicle requires six times the mineral inputs of a conventional car, and onshore wind requires nine times more than a natural gas plant. Bourgoin described the shift as a move from a fuel-intensive energy system to a mineral- and land-intensive “energy addition” regime.

The expansion of these projects overlaps significantly with the territories of marginalized communities. According to the report, half of all transition mineral concessions—roughly 120 million hectares (297 million acres)—and 25% of utility-scale renewable energy projects overlap directly with the lands of Indigenous Peoples and local communities.

cards.headline: Trillium College students face selective return to classes following OSAP pause

pages.text: Students at Trillium College, an Ontario career college with five campuses, are expressing frustration over a selective return to classes. The school is allowing only students who can pay tuition without financial aid to continue learning, while others remain on a temporary academic pause. This follows a provincewide suspension of Ontario Student Assistance Program (OSAP) payments for students at private post-secondary institutions. OSAP is a government financial aid program that provides loans and grants to students to help cover tuition and living expenses. The pause was announced in early October by Colleges and Universities Minister Nolan Quinn during a government-commissioned audit of the sector, which Quinn stated uncovered serious and widespread concerns.

Trillium College had previously announced it was suspending classes due to uncertainty caused by the provincial government's OSAP pause. For many career colleges, OSAP-funded tuition represents a sizable portion of revenue, and some institutions have reported struggling, laying off staff, or considering closure. While certain student cohorts have begun returning to class, the school has informed students that those without an eligible funding source or an approved payment arrangement will remain on academic pause and will not return with their cohort. Under the school's payment plans, students must pay weekly in advance of the following week's classes; if a payment is missed, a student's attendance may be temporarily paused.

Lorraine Eaton, a student in the law and security program at Trillium College, said she was supposed to graduate in January and had a security guard job lined up. Because she relies completely on OSAP loans and cannot pay tuition out of pocket, she has been told she cannot attend class. Eaton noted that some classmates are currently in class while others have been removed from the teacher's class list. Minister Nolan Quinn has not provided a specific timeline for the resumption of OSAP, stating only that it would be in the new year. Additionally, low-interest, third-party bank loans that Quinn said he was attempting to arrange have not yet materialized.

cards.headline: New mathematical algorithms improve accuracy of brain activity recordings

pages.text: Three new computational algorithms developed by Merav Stern, a physics fellow at Rockefeller University, can more accurately reveal brain activity by correcting noisy calcium signals. Published in Cell Reports Methods, these tools aim to solve a data problem in wide-field calcium imaging, a common technique used to record brain activity across large cortical areas. This method is largely noninvasive and allows researchers to observe how behavior connects to brain activity using light. The process relies on changes in calcium levels that occur during cellular activity, often using a synthetic protein called GCaMP, which fluoresces neon green during the calcium shift.

The current imaging method has limitations because the calcium indicator only approximates the original neural activity. Stern, a theoretical physicist who uses mathematical modeling to study complex brain networks, compares the phenomenon to a firework: when a firework bursts, a cloud of smoke lingers afterward that only approximates the original explosion's shape, size, and origin. Similarly, when a neuron fires, the resulting change in calcium levels creates a fluorescent signal that acts as a proxy for brain activity, but it does not perfectly mirror the initial event. While neuroscientists have previously attempted to correct this using mathematical algorithms borrowed from astrophysics, Stern's new methods are designed to recover the actual neural activity, or the 'fireworks,' from the data.

Stern stated that all three of her new methods were superior to using fluorescence alone as a measure of the neural spiking rate. She noted that the algorithms offer a more reliable depiction of underlying neural dynamics. Because each algorithm possesses unique strengths, Stern said neuroscientists can choose the specific method that works best for their particular data set.

cards.headline: Winter rains deepen Gaza shelter, sanitation, and food security crisis

pages.text: Winter rains in Gaza are flooding makeshift shelters, destroying scarce food supplies, and leaving displaced families struggling to stay warm and fed. More than 1.7 million Gazans remain displaced, and 1.4 million face acute hunger. The United Nations' food and migration agencies warn that critical funding shortfalls and continued restrictions on humanitarian aid deliveries are placing additional pressure on an already fragile response. Recent improvements in food security remain precarious, as they are sustained mainly by humanitarian aid rather than any recovery in local food systems, markets, or livelihoods. Winter flooding and the destruction of food stocks risk reversing those gains.

Karl Baker, the regional crisis coordinator for the UN International Organization for Migration (IOM), stated that tens of thousands of shelters were damaged or destroyed after just one day of rain. The impact on safety has already resulted in fatalities: at least five people were killed by a collapsed sand bank just over a week ago, and humanitarian partners reported that two children died in fires accidentally started by families attempting to stay warm by cooking inside their tents. Shaun Hughes, the World Food Programme (WFP) country director for Palestine, reported that floodwater and sewage have destroyed food stocks stored in tents, while cooking gas and firewood are unavailable or unaffordable. Hughes noted that because most people burn rubbish to cook, the wetness of the rubbish has further complicated food preparation.

The humanitarian response is also facing significant reductions in service frequency. Shaun Hughes stated that in the tented camps for displaced families, the WFP previously provided one hot meal a day, but now provides one hot meal every two days. The scale of the damage from the rains has increased fears regarding how displaced families will withstand the upcoming winter months.

cards.headline: Asháninka Indigenous militias defend Peruvian Amazon against drug traffickers without state support

pages.text: Asháninka Indigenous communities in the Peruvian Amazon are using self-defence committees, known as Cads, to protect their territory from drug traffickers. These grassroots militias, which were previously armed by the Peruvian government to fight Maoist Shining Path (Sendero Luminoso) rebels during the country's internal conflict between 1980 and 2000, are now operating without similar assistance from the state. In the Poyeni community, the largest town on the Tambo River, Cad volunteers called ronderos maintain sentry posts to watch over the river and surrounding rainforest.

cards.headline: New poll suggests Torontonians are unenthusiastic about Waymo launch plans

pages.text: A new poll from Liaison Strategies suggests residents in the Greater Toronto Area are wary of plans by the ride-hailing platform Waymo to launch its services in the city. In mid-October, Waymo announced it had begun testing self-driving vehicles on Toronto roads to map the city ahead of a planned full-service launch in 2028. However, research from the pollster indicates significant resistance to the expansion of the autonomous vehicle service into Canada.

The Liaison Strategies research found that 62 per cent of those surveyed in Toronto would not be likely to use a Waymo. Additionally, only 36 per cent of those surveyed believe the service should be allowed to launch paid, driverless rides in Toronto at all. David Valentin, principal at Liaison Strategies, told CBC News that the results are not encouraging for Waymo, noting that only 11 per cent of respondents said the service should start.

cards.headline: Rising carbon dioxide levels decrease silicon and lower pH in Washington coastal waters

pages.text: A study by University of Chicago researchers shows that elevated carbon dioxide levels in a coastal ecosystem have led to a rapid decline in pH and a decrease in dissolved silicon. This reduction in silicon affects microscopic algae, which use the mineral to build their skeletons. Because these algae serve as the base of the ocean food chain, feeding much of the zooplankton and fish that support coastal fisheries, the changes pose risks to various species and human activities like fishing. The research was based on data collected from waters around Tatoosh Island, part of the Makah Tribal Nation off the northwest coast of Washington state.

The findings relate to ocean acidification, a process where the ocean absorbs up to 30% of emitted carbon dioxide. When carbon dioxide reacts with seawater, it lowers the pH, making the water more acidic. While many studies on acidification focus on how it makes it chemically harder and more energy-intensive for shellfish to produce and maintain calcium carbonate shells, this study highlights impacts on primary productivity in phytoplankton. Timothy Wootton, a professor of ecology and evolution at the University of Chicago, noted that the long-term data suggests this process is especially worrisome because it affects the very base of the food chain. Wootton and co-author Cathy Pfister, also a professor of ecology and evolution at the University of Chicago, have studied this ecosystem for more than 40 years, monitoring ocean chemistry and populations of fish, birds, mollusks, barnacles, and seaweeds.

cards.headline: Manitoba real estate trust proposes funding model to help federal government address homelessness

pages.text: The Collaborative Housing Alliance, a Manitoba real estate investment trust, says its funding model could be replicated to help the federal government meet its goal of building 2,000 new permanent supportive and transitional housing units in Winnipeg. The trust uses a pool of capital to fund the construction of affordable to mixed-market housing by paying for purchases, labour, or materials. This capital is raised through a combination of public and private sources, including donations and investments into the trust's real estate investment model. The organization can either work with a charity to co-own and develop a project or build housing directly, after which a non-profit group may lease the premises or take over tenant support, sometimes with the intention of eventually purchasing the property.

Over the past 12 months, the Collaborative Housing Alliance helped bring at least 62 housing spaces online through three Manitoba projects. This included 24 spaces in a West End building intended for people moving out of transitional housing. The organization started two years ago with $10 million in provincial funding. Tessa Blaikie Whitecloud, the president and CEO of the Collaborative Housing Alliance, said the organization has since raised approximately $11 million from the private sector through donations or investor funds. Blaikie Whitecloud stated that assistance from both the public and private sectors is necessary to build sufficient housing supply.

cards.headline: Mozambique opposition leader Venâncio Mondlane goes on trial in Maputo

pages.text: Venâncio Mondlane, a leader of the opposition in Mozambique, has appeared at the Supreme Court to face charges including incitement to terrorism and civil disobedience. The charges stem from deadly protests that followed the country's disputed 2024 elections. Mondlane denies any wrongdoing, and his party has described the trial as politically motivated. He arrived at the court early, stating to journalists that he arrived with “great peace of mind” and felt “confident in the work of my legal team.” He was greeted by dozens of supporters amid a heavy police presence in the capital, Maputo. Authorities maintained tight security due to fears of fresh demonstrations, leading many people to stay home and causing some businesses to remain closed. Police appealed to citizens to follow the proceedings calmly to avoid threatening public order.

The trial follows a period of intense political unrest after Mondlane challenged the 2024 presidential election results, which declared Daniel Chapo of the ruling Frelimo party the winner. Mondlane accused authorities of widespread electoral fraud and called for nationwide protests and work stoppages. These demonstrations continued for months, and rights groups accused security forces of using excessive force against protesters. Amnesty International, citing local civil society organisations, stated that more than 300 people were killed during the unrest, which was described as one of the country's worst post-election crises since independence. Political analyst Luis Nhachote noted that the trial serves as an important opportunity to demonstrate that the rule of law applies equally to everyone and acts as a test for Mozambique's political stability.

cards.headline: Scientists reconstruct history of 52,000-year-old runaway stars in Large Magellanic Cloud

pages.text: Astronomers believe they have resolved a long-standing mystery regarding a violent event that occurred approximately 52,000 years ago in the Large Magellanic Cloud, a dwarf galaxy orbiting the Milky Way. During this period, several large stars fled their original locations at high velocities following a cosmic skirmish. For years, the unusual trajectories and speeds of these runaway stars remained unexplained until new data allowed researchers to reconstruct the history of the altercation.

The breakthrough came from data provided by the European Southern Observatory (ESO) Gaia satellite, which has mapped the nearby heavens with high precision since its launch in 2013. Using this data, which includes precise measurements of the positions, masses, and velocities of the fugitive stars, Simon Portegies Zwart and colleagues were able to piece together the event. The findings offer new insights into the history of the local cosmos and the dynamics of stellar clusters, which are groups of stars held together by gravity.

cards.headline: Thailand and Myanmar signed a weakened river pollution agreement that has yet to produce results

pages.text: Thai Foreign Minister Sihasak Phuangketkeow visited Naypyidaw, the capital of Myanmar, on Nov. 12 to discuss trade, border security, and the pollution of Thai rivers caused by mining in Myanmar. While the Thai Ministry of Foreign Affairs reported that transboundary pollution from Myanmar mines was discussed, the visit highlighted a lack of progress on bilateral solutions to heavy metal contamination that has affected multiple rivers in northern Thailand since early 2025. Although representatives agreed to convene a joint working group and conduct a joint field visit, sources within the Thai Ministry of Foreign Affairs confirmed to Mongabay that the joint working group has not met once since the agreement was signed in August.

The agreement, a six-page document signed three months prior to the Nov. 12 visit, was intended to establish terms for jointly monitoring the transboundary water pollution crisis linked to unregulated mining in Myanmar. However, the agreement faced criticism from government officials and civil society before it was even signed. Critics warned that numerous revisions requested by Myanmar and accepted by Thailand meant the bilateral efforts would likely fail to provide meaningful relief for the tens of thousands of communities living downstream of the mining runoff.

For nearly two years, Thai authorities have detected dangerous levels of arsenic and other heavy metals in the water and sediment of the Kok, Sai, and Ruak rivers—a three-river system feeding into the Mekong River—as well as in the sediment of the Mekong itself. Additionally, the Salween River has been found at points over the last 20 months to be contaminated by chemicals linked by Thai authorities to Myanmar’s mines. In Thailand’s southern Ranong province, the Kraburi River has faced heavy siltation due to expanding illicit tin mining on the Myanmar side.

cards.headline: Pataxó Indigenous people protest arrest of female vice-chief in Bahia, Brazil

pages.text: Pataxó Indigenous people occupied the entrance of a Civil Police station in Eunápolis, in the far south of Brazil’s Bahia state, on Nov 12 to protest the arrest of two leaders from the Barra Velha Indigenous Territory. The peaceful demonstration followed the Nov 11 arrest of Erilsa Braz dos Santos, known as Uruba Pataxó, the vice-chief of Barra Velha Mother Village, and communicator Karen Pataxó. Both women were detained during Operation Barra Velha, an action carried out by the Civil and Military Police in the Porto Seguro municipality, on suspicion of drug trafficking in the region. The Pataxó deny these accusations.

While Karen Pataxó was released, Uruba Pataxó remained in custody and was transferred to a prison in Teixeira de Freitas on Nov 12. The transfer sparked social media mobilization and outrage among Indigenous people. Uruba Pataxó is a teacher, the secretary of the territory’s Council of Chiefs, and a regional coordinator of the United Movement of Indigenous Peoples and Organizations of Bahia (Mupoiba). Indigenous leader Dário Pataxó told Mongabay that the imprisonment is intended to silence those who speak out against drug trafficking in the territory. He noted that the movement has already seen the detention of [Cacique] Suruí, the former president of the Barra Velha Council of Chiefs, who is facing proceedings under house arrest.

During the Eunápolis demonstration, a protester stated in a video published on Instagram by the Media and Art Research Center (Nupomar) and Barra Velha Village that the arrest is a political accusation against a leader defending her people and territory. In a statement, Mupoiba described the situation as an orchestrated effort driven by forces serving rural militias and predatory large landholdings to persecute land defenders, noting that investigations into armed attacks against Indigenous communities are proceeding slowly.
